questions.title: Basic Console Greeting with Scanner
questions.question: Read a user's name from standard input using `java.util.Scanner` and print a personalized greeting to the console.
questions.explanation: Interactive console applications in Java typically obtain input via `java.util.Scanner` wrapping the standard input stream `System.in`. At runtime, `System.in` represents an open `InputStream` connected to the keyboard or parent terminal buffer. Initializing `new Scanner(System.in)` allows the application to parse tokens and lines using regular expressions. Calling `scanner.nextLine()` reads character bytes from the buffer until encountering a line feed (`\n`) or carriage return (`\r\n`), consuming the delimiter and returning the accumulated string. This introduces the input/output lifecycle, stream parsing, and string formatting in terminal programs.
hints: Instantiate `Scanner` with `System.in` as its constructor source.
Use `scanner.nextLine()` to read the entire user input string including spaces.
Print the prompt without a newline (`System.out.print`) to keep the cursor adjacent to the input prompt.
questions.expectedOutput:
Enter your name: Akshat
Hello, Akshat!

questions.title: Interactive Two-Integer Summation
questions.question: Prompt the user for two integers sequentially using `Scanner.nextInt()`, compute their arithmetic sum, and display the result.
questions.explanation: Parsing numeric primitives directly from terminal input is supported by `Scanner.nextInt()`. Under the hood, `Scanner` skips leading whitespace delimiters, matches digits against signed integer regular expressions according to the default locale, and converts the character stream into a 32-bit two's-complement integer primitive via `Integer.parseInt()`. If the user inputs non-numeric characters or a number that overflows the bounds of `Integer.MIN_VALUE` to `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, `Scanner` throws an `InputMismatchException`. This exercise highlights typed input consumption, operand accumulation, and stream pointer advancement.
hints: Call `scanner.nextInt()` sequentially for both the first and second integer operands.
Store the values in primitive `int` variables before computing their sum.
Remember that `nextInt()` only scans numeric tokens and leaves any subsequent newline delimiter in the stream.
questions.expectedOutput:
Enter first integer: 4
Enter second integer: 6
Sum: 10

questions.title: Circle Area Calculation from User Radius
questions.question: Read a floating-point radius value from console input using `Scanner.nextDouble()` and calculate the circle's area using `Math.PI` formatted to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Reading floating-point numbers requires `Scanner.nextDouble()`, which parses standard IEEE 754 64-bit precision values. The mathematical area of a circle is defined by $A = \pi r^2$. In Java, `Math.PI` provides the closest double-precision approximation of $\pi$. Because floating-point multiplication can introduce trailing binary precision artifacts, production applications format numerical output with `System.out.printf` using format specifiers like `%.2f` to round the display to two decimal places without altering the underlying numerical state.
hints: Use `scanner.nextDouble()` to read the radius into a primitive `double` variable.
Calculate the area using `Math.PI * radius * radius`.
Use `System.out.printf("Area: %.2f%n", area)` or `String.format()` to round the output to two decimal places.
questions.expectedOutput:
Enter radius: 7
Area: 153.94

questions.title: Full-Line Text Reader and Length Calculator
questions.question: Read an entire line of text including whitespace using `Scanner.nextLine()` and output the total number of characters in the entered string.
questions.explanation: Standard token-based methods in `Scanner` (`next()`, `nextInt()`) delimit input by whitespace, making them unsuitable for reading sentences or free-form strings. `Scanner.nextLine()` scans all characters until it reaches a newline boundary, returning the entire sequence without the trailing newline character. Calling `.length()` on the resulting `String` object returns the total count of 16-bit UTF-16 code units. This exercise helps students understand line-buffered input versus whitespace-delimited tokenization.
hints: Use `scanner.nextLine()` to capture spaces and punctuation within a single line.
Call `.length()` on the retrieved `String` reference to compute character length.
Handle empty lines gracefully, noting that an empty line returns a string of length 0.
questions.expectedOutput:
Enter a line of text: Java Backend Developer
Line: "Java Backend Developer"
Character count: 22

questions.title: Vowel Classification from Character Input
questions.question: Read a single character from the console using `scanner.next().charAt(0)` and determine whether it is an English vowel (A, E, I, O, U, case-insensitive).
questions.explanation: `Scanner` does not provide a native `nextChar()` method. Instead, character input is achieved by reading a single-word token using `scanner.next()` and extracting its initial character using `charAt(0)`. To perform case-insensitive classification, the character is converted to lowercase with `Character.toLowerCase(ch)`. A switch statement or condition checking against `'a'`, `'e'`, `'i'`, `'o'`, and `'u'` then classifies the letter. This pattern is standard for handling interactive menu choices, confirmation flags (Y/N), and character-based commands.
hints: Read the token via `scanner.next()` and extract index 0 with `.charAt(0)`.
Convert the character using `Character.toLowerCase(ch)` to eliminate casing branches.
Check whether the character matches 'a', 'e', 'i', 'o', or 'u'.

questions.title: Composite Profile Prompter
questions.question: Write a console program using `Scanner` that prompts for a user's name and age, then formats and displays: 'Hello [name], you are [age] years old!'.
questions.explanation: Interactive command-line wizards often collect multiple profile attributes in sequence. When prompting for a string followed by a numeric primitive, using `scanner.next()` or `scanner.nextLine()` reads the text token, and `scanner.nextInt()` parses the age. Because the string is read before the integer, no unconsumed newline issues occur. The values are then concatenated into a template message, demonstrating sequential input prompts and mixed-type data extraction from `System.in`.
hints: Read the name first using `scanner.nextLine()` or `scanner.next()`.
Read the integer age using `scanner.nextInt()`.
Interpolate the extracted variables into the final formatted output message.

Enter your age: 26
Hello Akshat, you are 26 years old!

questions.title: Scanner NextLine Trap Fix
questions.question: Demonstrate the `scanner.nextInt()` newline trap where trailing newline characters cause a subsequent `scanner.nextLine()` call to return empty, and implement the standard fix.
questions.explanation: A common pitfall with `java.util.Scanner` is the interaction between token-based methods (`nextInt()`, `nextDouble()`, `next()`) and line-based methods (`nextLine()`). Token methods scan and parse digits but do not consume the trailing newline (`\n`) generated when the user presses Enter. When `scanner.nextLine()` is subsequently called, it reads the remaining newline character from the buffer and returns an empty string immediately, skipping actual user input. The solution is to place a clearing call to `scanner.nextLine()` immediately after `nextInt()` to consume the leftover newline before reading the next line of text.
hints: Read the integer using `int age = scanner.nextInt();`.
Insert an extra `scanner.nextLine();` to consume the leftover newline delimiter from the buffer.
Read the full subsequent string using `String address = scanner.nextLine();`.
questions.expectedOutput:
Enter age: 26
Enter address: 742 Evergreen Terrace
Profile captured -> Age: 26 | Address: 742 Evergreen Terrace

questions.title: Running Total and Average Sentinel Loop
questions.question: Repeatedly prompt the user to enter integers until they enter the sentinel value `0`, then display the total sum and calculated average of all entered values.
questions.explanation: Sentinel-controlled loops process streams of arbitrary length when the total number of inputs is unknown in advance. The program maintains an accumulator (`sum`) and a counter (`count`) inside a `while (true)` loop. On each iteration, an integer is parsed. If the input matches the sentinel value (`0`), the loop terminates via `break`. If no values were entered before `0`, the program avoids division by zero; otherwise, it computes the average by casting `sum` to a `double`. This pattern is fundamental to command-line accumulators, batch transaction entry, and streaming calculations.
hints: Maintain running totals: `int sum = 0;` and `int count = 0;`.
Inspect the input: if `val == 0`, break out of the input loop.
Cast `sum` to `double` before dividing by `count` to preserve decimal precision in the average.

Enter number (0 to finish): 20
Enter number (0 to finish): 30
Enter number (0 to finish): 0

Total sum: 60
Average: 20.00

questions.title: Character Input and Boolean Confirmation Flag
questions.question: Prompt the user for a single confirmation character (Y/N) using `scanner.next().charAt(0)`, validate the character, and display the corresponding boolean decision.
questions.explanation: Interactive confirmation prompts require validating user input against acceptable command choices. By extracting `charAt(0)` from `scanner.next()`, the application isolates the first character entered, ignoring any extra characters typed before pressing Enter. Normalizing the character with `Character.toUpperCase(ch)` allows the validator to accept both `'y'` and `'Y'` as true, and `'n'` and `'N'` as false. Any other character can be rejected as invalid input, illustrating robust character-based decision handling.
hints: Read the choice with `char response = scanner.next().charAt(0);`.
Convert to uppercase using `char upper = Character.toUpperCase(response);`.
Check for `'Y'` or `'N'` and print whether the confirmation succeeded.

questions.title: BufferedReader Console Reader
questions.question: Implement user input collection using `BufferedReader` and `InputStreamReader` instead of `Scanner`, reading two text lines and handling `IOException`.
questions.explanation: `BufferedReader` paired with `InputStreamReader` is Java's traditional, high-throughput mechanism for reading character streams. While `Scanner` performs regex parsing and type conversions on an 8 KB buffer, `BufferedReader` uses a 16 KB default buffer and reads raw strings directly via `readLine()`, making it significantly faster for competitive programming and high-volume I/O. However, `BufferedReader.readLine()` throws checked `IOException`s that must be caught or declared, does not parse numeric tokens automatically, and returns `null` when the end of stream is reached.
hints: Wrap `System.in` in `new InputStreamReader(...)` and wrap that in `new BufferedReader(...)`.

questions.title: Batch Integer Summary Statistics
questions.question: Read an integer `N`, followed by `N` integers. Compute and display the maximum value, minimum value, and calculated average of the sequence.
questions.explanation: Processing a fixed-size batch of numbers requires reading a count `N` followed by a bounded loop. To track extremes accurately without arbitrary boundaries, the first integer is read outside the loop (or on the first iteration) to initialize both `max` and `min`. On subsequent iterations, `Math.max()` and `Math.min()` update the extrema while an accumulator computes the running sum. When all `N` values are processed, the average is calculated as `(double) sum / n`. This avoids integer truncation and teaches robust extrema tracking.
hints: Read `int n = scanner.nextInt();` to determine iteration count.
Read the first value to initialize both `min` and `max`.
Loop `n - 1` times to read remaining values, updating `min`, `max`, and `sum`.

Min: -5
Average: 25.00

questions.title: Mixed-Mode Age and Full Name Parser
questions.question: Read an integer age using `nextInt()`, followed by a multi-word full name using `nextLine()`, consuming the leftover newline delimiter to capture both values correctly.
questions.explanation: Mixed-mode scanning combines token-based numeric reading with whitespace-sensitive line reading. When `scanner.nextInt()` processes numeric characters, it stops at the first trailing delimiter (usually `\n`), leaving it in the stream buffer. A subsequent call to `scanner.nextLine()` reads that remaining newline and returns an empty string immediately. Inserting an empty `scanner.nextLine()` call discards the leftover delimiter, allowing the second `scanner.nextLine()` to wait for and read the actual full name entered by the user.
hints: Parse the numeric age with `scanner.nextInt()`.

questions.title: Sentinel Value Accumulator
questions.question: Continuously read integers from the console until the user inputs `0`, then output the count of non-zero entries and their aggregate sum.
questions.explanation: A sentinel loop terminates execution when a designated stopping value (the sentinel) is encountered. In this problem, `0` serves as the sentinel marker. The application loops while reading input, checking each value against `0`. If non-zero, the value is added to an accumulator and a counter is incremented; if `0`, the loop terminates. Sentinel loops are useful when processing streaming input of unknown length without requiring a separate pre-count parameter.

questions.title: Guarded Range Integer Validator
questions.question: Repeatedly prompt the user for an integer between 1 and 100, using `scanner.hasNextInt()` to reject non-numeric input and discarding invalid tokens until a valid number is supplied.
questions.explanation: Robust CLI applications validate user input defensively to prevent crashes from invalid types or out-of-range values. `scanner.hasNextInt()` inspects the next token without consuming it, returning `false` if the token cannot be parsed as an integer. When non-numeric input is detected, `scanner.next()` consumes and discards the invalid token. When a valid integer is found, the program checks whether it falls within the required range `[1, 100]`. The prompt repeats until an acceptable value is entered, making the input loop resilient against malformed data.

questions.title: Input Type Guardian
questions.question: Implement an input validation method using `scanner.hasNextInt()` in a loop to discard non-numeric tokens and re-prompt until a valid integer is supplied.
questions.explanation: Type validation ensures that console input matches the expected data type before parsing. Instead of catching `InputMismatchException` using try-catch blocks (which can carry performance overhead in tight loops), `scanner.hasNextInt()` checks the token type beforehand. When `hasNextInt()` returns `false`, calling `scanner.next()` consumes the invalid token, preventing an infinite loop. Once `hasNextInt()` returns `true`, calling `scanner.nextInt()` safely retrieves the integer without throwing an exception.

questions.title: Secure Password Prompt with Console Fallback
questions.question: Implement password collection using `System.console().readPassword()` to mask input characters, providing a fallback to `Scanner` when running inside an IDE where `System.console()` is null.
questions.explanation: Reading sensitive credentials with standard `Scanner` or `System.in` echoes plain-text characters directly to the terminal display, exposing them in console logs and over-the-shoulder viewing. `System.console().readPassword()` disables terminal echo and returns a `char[]` rather than an immutable `java.lang.String`. Using a `char[]` allows the application to overwrite password characters with zeros (`Arrays.fill(pwd, '0')`) immediately after use, preventing secrets from lingering in heap dumps. In IDE execution environments, `System.console()` often returns `null`, so robust applications include a fallback to `Scanner`.
hints: Check if `System.console() != null` before invoking `readPassword()`.
Fall back to `new Scanner(System.in).nextLine().toCharArray()` if console is null.

questions.title: Non-Blocking Console Listener

The `available()` method returns an estimate of unread bytes currently waiting in the OS input buffer without blocking. If `available() > 0`, input is present and can be read immediately; if it returns `0`, the thread can continue executing background tasks and sleep periodically without freezing the application.

questions.question: Implement an interactive command shell that reads commands with arguments (e.g., `echo "Hello World"`, `set key val`), parses quoted substrings into single tokens, and executes registered handlers.
questions.explanation: Standard string splitting using `split(" ")` breaks quoted strings containing spaces, corrupting arguments like `echo "Hello World"`. Building a shell tokenizer requires parsing the input character by character using state machine logic: tracking whether the current character is inside double quotes, handling escape sequences (`\\`), and appending characters to an active token buffer. When an unquoted space is encountered, the current token is emitted and a new one begins. The command verb (token 0) is then dispatched to registered command handlers, mirroring the behavior of command-line shells like Bash.
hints: Iterate character by character, tracking an `inQuotes` boolean flag.
Only treat spaces as token delimiters when `inQuotes` is `false`.
Dispatch token 0 as the command name and pass remaining tokens as arguments.
questions.expectedOutput:
Command: echo "Welcome to Java Shell" --verbose
Parsed Tokens: [echo, Welcome to Java Shell, --verbose]
Echo Output: Welcome to Java Shell

questions.title: Automated Input Stream Testing Harness
questions.question: Implement an automated unit testing harness that mocks interactive user input using `System.setIn()` with a `ByteArrayInputStream`, captures `System.out` via `ByteArrayOutputStream`, and validates program behavior.
questions.explanation: Testing interactive CLI applications in automated build pipelines requires redirecting standard I/O streams programmatically. By calling `System.setIn(new ByteArrayInputStream(simulatedBytes))`, test harnesses feed predetermined input to components that read from `System.in`. Similarly, `System.setOut(new PrintStream(outputCaptureStream))` intercepts console output, allowing assertions against the displayed text. Crucially, original stream references (`System.in` and `System.out`) must be restored in a `finally` block to prevent test pollution in shared JVM test environments.
hints: Save original streams: `InputStream origIn = System.in;` and `PrintStream origOut = System.out;`.
Redirect input using `System.setIn(new ByteArrayInputStream(...))`.
Always restore original streams in a `finally` block after running assertions.
questions.expectedOutput:
Harness captured output: Enter code: PROCESSED_789
Assertion passed: true

questions.title: Interactive Matrix Input Engine with Line-by-Line Token Validation
questions.question: Prompt the user for matrix dimensions $R$ and $C$, then validate each row of space-separated tokens, handling irregular row lengths and parsing errors with line re-prompts.
questions.explanation: Validating multidimensional matrix input requires handling irregular row lengths, missing elements, and malformed numeric tokens. This problem reads dimensions $R$ and $C$, then uses a line-oriented validation loop for each row. The program reads entire lines using `scanner.nextLine()`, splits tokens by whitespace, and checks that the count matches $C$ exactly. Each token is then parsed to an integer inside a `try-catch` block. If a row has too few tokens or contains non-numeric characters, the entire row is rejected, and the user is prompted to re-enter that specific row without discarding previously validated rows.
hints: Read each row as a full line using `scanner.nextLine()` to avoid buffer alignment issues.
Verify `tokens.length == c` before parsing numeric values.
Wrap `Integer.parseInt()` in a `try-catch` block and retry the current row index if parsing fails.
